newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi leader asks workers to back war effort.
newsitem.headline: Burundi leader asks workers to back war effort.

text.p: Burundi's military leader told the country's workers on Saturday they might have dip into their shrinking pay packets to finance the war effort against Hutu rebels.

Major Pierre Buyoya briefed Burundi's 26 trades unions and the employers' federation about the critical state of the economy more than two months after regional states imposed a total trade and transport embargo.

"Please do not ask for salary increases now. Instead, in the days to come, we may ask for your contribution to help finance the war," Buyoya told the union leaders in the Kirundi language, according to an unofficial translation.
The economic sanctions were imposed on July 31 as punishment for the mainly Tutsi army's putsch six days earlier.
The new regime says the embargo has cost Burundi more than $130 million. The economy, almost starved of fuel and with no revenue from blocked coffee exports, is barely working.
But the priority for Burundi's 15 percent Tutsi minority is not to lose the guerrilla war with Hutu rebels whom the army says are infiltrating from Zaire and Tanzania.

Buyoya told Reuters on Thursday the guerrillas could not win but diplomatic and humanitarian sources say they are keeping the army at full stretch. A senior diplomat put the army's strength at 28,000 after recent recruitment drives.
Anicet Niyongabo, a leader of the 2,000-strong textile and leather workers' union, said there was broad agreement with Buyoya at the meeting.
"We are conscious of the need for a contribution to the war effort.
"But the funds must be properly managed so that workers are satisfied that they will help to bring peace," Niyongabo told reporters.
He denied the unions mainly represented urbanised Tutsis and not the majority Hutus.
"Even if Burundian society is very polarised, the embargo affects Hutus and Tutsis in the same way," he said.
Regional leaders have told Buyoya to enter unconditional negotiations with Hutu rebels if he wants the embargo lifted.
Despite the risk of dissent among Tutsi hardliners, Buyoya has agreed to such talks in principle. Niyongabo said the precise nature of negotiations had to be debated in advance.
"We must negotiate peace, not death," he said, reflecting Tutsi fears that the rebels will slaughter the minority if they are allowed to take control.
Civil servants have so far kept their jobs and been paid on time but lay-offs are increasing in the private sector.
Niyongabo said at Burundi's largest textile factory, where he is one 1,200 employees, fuel shortages have led to reduced working hours and pay.

About 400 people attended a mass on Saturday at Bujumbura's Regina Mundi cathedral in memory of Archbishop Joachim Ruhuna, Burundi's Roman Catholic primate, who was murdered with two nuns in an ambush last September 9.
Buyoya's government said the rebels killed Ruhuna, a Tutsi.
